subtagline: Explore how cryptographic hash functions operate through interactive visual simulations. Master the core properties of SHA-256 that secure modern blockchains.

live_widget.badge: Live SHA-256 — type any characters in real time

home.properties_subtitle: These mathematical properties establish the cryptographic foundation of modern blockchains.
home.prop1_desc: SHA-256 always produces exactly 256 bits (64 hexadecimal characters), regardless of input size — from 1 byte to 1 terabyte.
home.prop2_desc: It is computationally infeasible to reconstruct the original input from the output hash. This forms the bedrock of modern digital security.
home.prop3_desc: Flipping a single bit or character causes ~50% of all output bits to change unpredictably and pseudo-randomly.
home.prop4_desc: The probability of finding two distinct inputs producing the identical output hash is practically zero.

hash_interaction.title: SHA-256 Hash Generator
hash_interaction.subtitle: Type any text and watch the SHA-256 hash update in real time
hash_interaction.tip_text: Flipping a single character causes the entire output hash to change completely — this is the Avalanche Effect. The hash output always maintains exactly 64 characters.

hash_fixed_length.title: Fixed Length Property
hash_fixed_length.subtitle: SHA-256 always produces exactly 64 hex characters (256 bits), regardless of input size.
hash_fixed_length.conclusion: All outputs are exactly 64 hex characters = 256 bits — the "fixed output length" property.

hash_avalanche.title: Avalanche Effect
hash_avalanche.subtitle: Change just 1 character and watch ~50% of the hash change completely.

theory_hash.title: SHA-256 Hash Function Theory
theory_hash.subtitle: Discover the mathematical principles, algorithm architecture, and the 4 core security properties of SHA-256.

what_is_hash.title: What is a Cryptographic Hash Function?
what_is_hash.desc: A cryptographic hash function is a deterministic mathematical algorithm that maps data of arbitrary size to a fixed-size bit string — known as a hash value or message digest.
what_is_hash.example_1tb: SHA256("1 TB file") → also exactly 64 hex characters (256 bits)

fixed_length.title: Fixed Output Length
fixed_length.desc: SHA-256 always generates exactly 256 bits = 32 bytes = 64 hexadecimal characters, regardless of whether the input is a single letter or a multi-terabyte dataset.
fixed_length.sub: This property guarantees predictable memory storage and enables constant-time verification across distributed blockchain networks.

one_way.title: One-Way Function (Pre-image Resistance)
one_way.desc: Reversing a hash digest is computationally infeasible — it is impossible to recover the original input x given only the output hash H such that SHA256(x) = H.
one_way.sub: With 2^256 possible outputs, finding the preimage via brute force would take longer than the estimated lifespan of the observable universe.

avalanche.title: Avalanche Effect
avalanche.desc: Flipping even a single bit in the input data (such as toggling case or adding a period) causes ~50% (approx. 128/256 bits) of the output digest to change completely at random.
avalanche.sub: This prevents statistical analysis and stops adversaries from detecting any correlations between similar inputs.

collision_resistance.title: Collision Resistance
collision_resistance.desc: It is practically impossible to find two distinct inputs x ≠ y that yield the identical hash output SHA256(x) = SHA256(y).
collision_resistance.sub: Under the Birthday Paradox, finding a collision requires approximately 2^128 operations — rendering SHA-256 mathematically secure against all modern computing power.

merkle_tree.title: Merkle Tree & Merkle Root Architecture
merkle_tree.desc: A Merkle Tree is a binary tree of concatenated cryptographic hashes that summarizes thousands of individual transactions into a single cryptographic root hash (Merkle Root).
merkle_tree.root_desc: The Merkle Root is embedded into the Block Header to ensure the tamper-evident integrity of all transactions in the block.
merkle_tree.spv_desc: Enables Simplified Payment Verification (SPV) with logarithmic O(log2 N) proof size, allowing lightweight clients to verify transactions without downloading entire blocks.

theory_mining.title: Mining Theory & Proof of Work
theory_mining.subtitle: Understand how miners solve cryptographic Proof-of-Work puzzles, the role of Nonces, dynamic difficulty adjustments, and blockchain immutability.

what_is_mining.title: What is Mining?
what_is_mining.desc: Mining is the computational process of finding a valid Nonce value (an integer starting from 0) such that hashing the serialized block header produces a digest starting with the required number of leading zeros.

what_is_nonce.title: What is a Nonce?
what_is_nonce.desc_1: Nonce (Number used ONCE) is the sole variable field miners are permitted to increment in the Block Header, starting from 0 upwards until finding a valid hash.
what_is_nonce.desc_2: Because SHA-256 is pseudo-random, the required Nonce cannot be predicted analytically. This brute-force search is why mining requires substantial compute energy.

difficulty_mechanics.title: How Network Difficulty Works
difficulty_mechanics.desc: Network difficulty dictates the mandatory number of leading hexadecimal zeros in the block hash. Each additional zero increases the average required search attempts by a factor of 16 (hexadecimal base).

difficulty_adjustment.title: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment Algorithm
difficulty_adjustment.desc: In Bitcoin, every 2016 blocks (~2 weeks), the protocol evaluates actual elapsed time against the target duration (20160 minutes = 14 days) to adjust difficulty up or down, maintaining an average 10-minute block interval.

blockchain_immutability.title: Blockchain Immutability & Chain Integrity
blockchain_immutability.desc: Every block stores the cryptographic hash of its predecessor (Previous Block Hash). Altering even a single byte in an old block changes its hash and invalidates the cryptographic linkage of all subsequent blocks.

attack_51.title: 51% Attack Vulnerability
attack_51.desc: If a mining entity gains control over >50% of the network hashrate, they can privately mine an alternate longer chain to re-organize historical blocks and execute double-spending attacks.

theory_rsa.title: RSA Cryptography & Digital Signature Theory
theory_rsa.subtitle: Master public/private key pairs, the 5 mathematical steps of RSA key generation, and digital signature mechanisms securing transactions.

asymmetric_overview.title: What is Asymmetric Encryption?
asymmetric_overview.desc: Unlike symmetric encryption relying on a single shared key, RSA uses a mathematically linked key pair: a Public Key for encryption and a Private Key for decryption.

public_key.title: Public Key
bullets: Used by senders to encrypt messages for the recipient
Used by verifiers to validate the owner's digital signatures
Mathematically impossible to deduce the private key from it

private_key.title: Private Key
private_key.sub: Strictly confidential, held only by the owner
bullets: Must remain strictly secret and never shared
Used to decrypt ciphertexts encrypted with the corresponding Public Key
Used to generate digital signatures for transactions
Loss of the Private Key results in permanent loss of asset ownership

five_steps.title: 5 Mathematical Steps for RSA Key Generation
five_steps.step1_title: Step 1: Choose two distinct prime numbers p and q
five_steps.step1_desc: Select two large random prime numbers: p and q (typically 2048 to 4096 bits in production environments).
five_steps.step2_title: Step 2: Calculate Modulus n = p × q
five_steps.step2_desc: n is published as part of both the Public and Private keys. The bit length of n represents the key size.
five_steps.step3_desc: φ(n) represents the count of positive integers less than n that are coprime to n. This value must be kept strictly confidential.
five_steps.step4_desc: Select e such that 1 < e < φ(n) and gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1 (standard choices: Fermat prime e = 65537 or 3, 17).
five_steps.step5_title: Step 5: Compute Private Exponent d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n)
five_steps.step5_desc: d is the modular multiplicative inverse of e modulo φ(n), calculated via the Extended Euclidean Algorithm such that (d × e) mod φ(n) = 1.

digital_signature.title: RSA Digital Signature Mechanism
digital_signature.desc: A digital signature is a mathematical scheme validating data integrity, signer authentication, and non-repudiation of transactions.
digital_signature.signing_formula: Signing: S = Hash(M)^d mod n (using Private Key)
digital_signature.verifying_formula: Verification: Hash' = S^e mod n (using Public Key). If Hash' == Hash(M) → Signature is valid.

real_world.title: Real-World Applications of Asymmetric Cryptography
real_world.ssl_tls: HTTPS / SSL / TLS encryption for secure web browsing and banking transactions.
real_world.ssh: Secure passwordless remote server shell authentication (SSH Key Pairs).
real_world.wallets: Cryptocurrency wallet addresses (Bitcoin, Ethereum) and blockchain transaction signing.

rsa_math.step1_title: Choose two prime numbers p and q
rsa_math.phi_hint: 💡 φ(n) (phi): counts integers coprime to n in range [1, n). This is RSA's "secret number".
rsa_math.e_condition: Condition: 1 < e < φ(n) = {phi} and gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1
rsa_math.step4_title: Compute private exponent d — Extended Euclid

rsa_real_world.title: RSA-2048 In Your Browser
rsa_real_world.subtitle: Using Web Crypto API to generate a real 2048-bit RSA key pair, encrypt and decrypt directly in the browser — nothing sent to the server.
rsa_real_world.key_pair_desc: Public key and Private key are ready. You can generate a new key pair at any time.
rsa_real_world.security_desc: All encryption happens in your browser. Keys and data are never sent to any server. Web Crypto API uses CPU hardware acceleration when available.
rsa_real_world.decrypt_error: [Error: Cannot decrypt this ciphertext with the Private Key]

rsa_digital_signature.notice_title: This demo uses RSA — real Blockchain uses ECDSA
rsa_digital_signature.notice_desc: In practice, Bitcoin uses ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm). This demo uses RSA-2048 to illustrate the concept as it is easier to understand.
rsa_digital_signature.title: Digital Signature & Blockchain
rsa_digital_signature.subtitle: Blockchain doesn't sign the full transaction data — only its hash. This makes verification faster and more secure.
rsa_digital_signature.why_hash: Why only sign the hash? RSA signatures can only process small data (a few KB). By signing the Merkle Root hash (32 bytes), you authenticate the entire block even with thousands of transactions.
rsa_digital_signature.sig_valid_desc: The message is unaltered and signed by the correct private key
rsa_digital_signature.sig_invalid_desc: The message has been altered or the signature does not match the Public Key!
rsa_digital_signature.callout_desc: In Bitcoin/Ethereum, senders sign transactions with their private key (usually ECDSA, a variant of RSA). The entire network verifies signatures with the public key — no trusted third party needed. This is the foundation of "trustless" in crypto.
